In March 2024, a severe connectivity issue struck the exchange shortly before the opening bell, disrupting premarket trading and impairing the software system responsible for matching buy and sell orders for more than two hours. Shares of Nasdaq, which lists Apple (AAPL.O) , Tesla (TSLA.O) and Nvidia (NVDA.O) among thousands of other companies, were unaffected by the network disruption. They have fallen about 3.8% so far in 2026.

item.title: Israel says commercial goods no longer entering Gaza after merchants suspend coordination
item.description: Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid. COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods. It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash. Hamas later said that the 10,000 shekel fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory. A majority of Gazans are dependent on aid supplies, following three years of war, repeated displacement and severe restrictions imposed by Israel on aid deliveries. A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two thirds of Gazans could face acute hunger by the year-end. Around 2 million Gazans live in the territory, most in makeshift shelters. Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, said that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing. COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300 — or half. Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar said the figure was closer to 300, with two thirds carrying commercial goods. Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies. ($1 = 3.1038 shekels)

item.title: ASML's 'sold out' outlook forces investors to look beyond demand
item.description: In April, computer chip equipment maker ASML's CEO Christophe Fouquet told shareholders that Europe's most valuable company would avoid becoming the chip industry's bottleneck "by all possible means".
item.dc:creator: Toby Sterling, Nathan Vifflin
item.content:encoded: In April, computer chip equipment maker ASML's CEO Christophe Fouquet told shareholders that Europe's most valuable company would avoid becoming the chip industry's bottleneck "by all possible means". Six months later, Fouquet acknowledged ASML's supply of chip-printing tools used to make the advanced logic and memory chips powering the AI boom will [USN:L6N4600AA TEXT:"fall short"] of demand in both 2027 and 2028. For customers, investors and ASML, whose shares have risen nearly 70% this year, the focus is shifting to whether the company can increase capacity fast enough to profit from the huge demand. At the same time, market jitters are increasing over the durability of the AI boom and forecasts that stretch years into the future. "ASML itself is now the bottleneck," said Han Dieperink, chief investment officer at wealth management firm Aureus, which holds ASML shares, adding that management was openly acknowledging that planned 30% capacity additions in 2027 and in 2028 will not be enough. Dieperink said discussions about future orders were already extending into 2029 and 2030, which he viewed as evidence that demand could continue to outstrip supply well beyond the current cycle. THE VALUATION DEBATE ASML's plans to address the backlog include shortening assembly times, upgrading machines already operating in the field and introducing faster models. It had planned to raise annual capacity to 110 of its $200 million EUV lithography machines by 2028, but is now looking at adding perhaps a dozen more. It is also expanding manufacturing capacity in [USN:L6N4510PI TEXT:"Eindhoven"], although the first phase is not expected to come online until 2029. Fouquet reassured investors on one point on Wednesday: ASML's own supply chain, including key optical systems supplier Zeiss, is not the limiting factor. Investors say uncertainties increase after 2028 and the company's valuation reflects that. Since June, even as financial analysts ratcheted up earnings estimates, ASML's stock price drifted lower on a relative basis to its future earnings. Mark Sloan, Senior Analyst at Stonehage Fleming, whose Global Best Ideas fund has a 3.5% position in ASML, said a decline in the company's valuation to about 30 times forward earnings from more than 45 times in June had made the stock attractive given its growth prospects and market dominance. "We are watching AI adoption and innovation, along with capital spending plans at key customers closely," he said. "We believe supply rather than demand is likely to remain ASML's key constraint." ASML has said it will also benefit from price increases in 2027 and 2028. AI SELLOFF FEARS Not all investors are convinced. Sceptics question whether the surge in spending on AI infrastructure will ultimately generate returns that justify the billions of dollars being invested today. Chip stocks have also [USN:L6N4610MM TEXT:"come under pressure"] from concerns that higher interest rates could make financing large AI and data-centre projects more difficult. The cost of insuring against defaults in the US technology sector hit [USN:L1N46104Z TEXT:"record highs"] on Thursday. Jefferies analyst Janardan Menon said concerns about financing AI investment, along with constraints on data-centre expansion such as power availability, could weigh on ASML. Its shares fell 5% on Thursday as part of a broader market selloff. "The primary factor driving this derating is scepticism about very high 2028 and 2029 expectations," said Menon, adding ASML's price-to-earnings ratio could fall into the low 20s during a downturn. WE DON'T WANT TO SAY 'WE'RE SOLD OUT' ASML's customers continue to jockey for access to its unrivaled high-end chipmaking tools. The company is now demanding sizeable down payments on orders, which CFO Roger Dassen said are "enough to hurt" if customers later try to cancel. Top customer TSMC (2330.TW) , which makes chips for Nvidia (NVDA.O) and Apple (AAPL.O) , said in July it did not expect equipment supply to constrain its expansion plans. It maintained 2026 capital spending plans of $60 billion to $64 billion [USN:L1N461004 TEXT:"on Thursday"]. Samsung (005930.KS) , SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Micron (MU.O) have also been booking ASML capacity amid strong demand for AI memory chips. Potential new customers could add further pressure. Elon Musk's proposed TeraFab project, which has yet to produce its first chip, could emerge as a significant buyer of advanced tools, while US restrictions on China remain a risk for sales of ASML's mid-range DUV tools. China is expected to account for about 20% of ASML's sales this year. Despite strong demand, ASML is holding off on accepting orders for 2029 and 2030 while it assesses both customers' readiness and its own ability to meet future demand. "We don't want now to accept orders from customer A, B, and C and then to tell customer D, who hasn't given orders yet for 2029 and 2030, sorry, we're sold out," Dassen told analysts on the post-earnings call.

item.title: How Aramco learned to keep pumping oil under fire
item.description: When attack drones struck Saudi Aramco's biggest oil pipeline last month, satellite images showed one of its pumping stations burnt to ashes. By the next day, scores of bulldozers were already building a new pipeline.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Zhdannikov
item.content:encoded: When attack drones struck Saudi Aramco's (2222.SE) biggest oil pipeline last month, satellite images showed one of its pumping stations burnt to ashes. By the next day, scores of bulldozers were already building a new pipeline. Within days pumping resumed. The speed of the recovery illustrates how the world's biggest oil producer has transformed its ability to operate under attack after years of assaults on energy infrastructure across the region. "Today, our teams can handle multiple incidents simultaneously, and we continue to build this capability," Saudi state oil firm Aramco's chief executive Amin Nasser told Reuters in an interview last week. Nasser said Aramco has built specialised rapid-response teams, expanded emergency stockpiles for repairs and deployed drones to assess damage even while incidents are still unfolding. Lessons on how to operate under fire came after drones and missiles hit Aramco's major oil processing facility in Abqaiq in 2019, temporarily knocking out half of Aramco's production. "After Abqaiq in 2019, we came up with the idea of rapid response teams, or what we call zero-hour responders," Nasser said. The company, long-viewed as one of the most technically advanced oil producers, then began to prepare for the possibility of multiple attacks on its facilities at the same time, Nasser said. Those capabilities have been repeatedly tested since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February this year and Iran and its proxies retaliated with strikes that hit Middle Eastern [USN:L6N4610JI TEXT:"infrastructure"]. The firm's crisis-management capabilities were tested again on Tuesday when a Houthi attack struck the company's headquarters complex, [USN:L6N4600QH TEXT:"causing extensive damage"]. DRONES AND WAREHOUSES SPEED RECOVERY Saudi daily oil output dropped below 7 million barrels for most of the first six months of the war, down from over 10 million barrels before the war, according to data from the International Energy Agency. Like other Gulf producers, Saudi Arabia's oil exports have been constrained by attacks on tankers and a shortage of ships restricting crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Yet Aramco has managed to repair damaged facilities and restore operations quickly thanks to specialised response teams, years of contingency planning, drone technology and abundant spare parts. Technology has allowed Aramco to compress the time between an attack and the start of repairs, Nasser said. The company's response to incidents was now more than six times faster than the industry average, he added, meaning it often takes just days to restart a facility even after significant damage. Normally, oil firms first contain an incident and then assess the damage, but Aramco begins assessment with drones while an incident is still unfolding, Nasser said. "Inspection drones provide an exceptional level of visibility and detail," Nasser said. "By the time the situation is under control, we are ready to get to work." Response teams can quickly send repair materials to a site before work begins, Nasser said. Some 90% of materials needed for repairs are produced locally or held in a local warehouse as Aramco has spent years building up supply chains and inventories. The ability to maintain production despite repeated attacks has become an important selling point with Aramco's customers, Nasser said. "They see that Aramco is able to deliver under different scenarios." While Saudi oil production recovered to about 8 million barrels a day in September, export routes remain vulnerable to disruptions beyond Aramco's control. The company is studying possible alternative routes to the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and Suez, Nasser said, without elaborating. "Details will be disclosed if and when a final decision is made," he said.

item.title: FBI, US Postal Service investigate suspicious mailings to election officials, lawmakers
item.description: The FBI and US Postal Service's law enforcement arm said on Thursday they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials and lawmakers' offices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: The FBI and US Postal Service's law enforcement arm said on Thursday they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials and lawmakers' offices ahead of the November 3 [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]. The FBI said some of the letters contained an unknown substance. A spokesperson for Senator Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said his office received a notification from the FBI that the US Postal Service intercepted a letter containing a suspicious substance mailed to one of Padilla's offices. Brendan Donahue, a deputy chief inspector with the US Postal Inspection Service, said some of the letters had been intercepted and that an investigation was ongoing. "We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue told reporters. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said late on Wednesday a series of suspicious letters was sent to state election offices. The US House of Representatives sergeant at arms, the House's chief law enforcement officer, told staff in an email seen by Reuters that some letters containing suspicious white powder substances were received by public officials. Earlier on Thursday, US Postmaster General David Steiner said USPS was "absolutely ready" to handle millions of ballots for the midterm elections that will determine control of the US Congress and other key races. POSTAL SERVICE PLANS NEW MEASURES The Postal Service said this month it would take "extraordinary measures" for the 2026 election, including extending hours at some retail locations and expediting handling, extra deliveries and special pickups of ballots. The extraordinary measures start October 24 "to expedite completed ballots to election offices during the final stretch of the election season," Steiner said, adding they include "local turnaround to bypass all processing when it's absolutely necessary to get ballots on time." On September 14, the US Supreme Court declined to let USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail. USPS said it would not enforce the rule under the order. The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting. In 2024, USPS delivered 99.2 million ballots to and from voters in the presidential election. About 30% of votes were cast by mail in the November 2024 presidential election, down from 46% in 2020. Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would benefit Republicans because Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to various surveys. Under the rule that was blocked, states would have had to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients to USPS and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. The Postal Service could then have refused to send out ballots that did not comply or were associated with voters not appearing on the lists.

item.title: US regional lender First Horizon to offload $4.5 billion of consumer mortgages
item.description: First Horizon said on Thursday it had struck a deal to sell about $4.5 billion of select lower-yielding consumer mortgages, as the US regional lender looks to boost its earnings.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: First Horizon (FHN.N) said on Thursday it had struck a deal to sell about $4.5 billion of select lower-yielding consumer mortgages, as the US regional lender looks to boost its earnings. Shares of the Memphis, Tennessee-based bank, which jumped 4% in morning trading, have slipped 5% this year as of last close. Here are some other details: The realignment of the mortgage business is part of a broader push by First Horizon to overhaul its balance sheet and focus on core customers. The residential mortgage loan sale will improve the bank's loan-to-deposit ratio, free up balance sheet capacity and support share buybacks. "The strategic actions clean up the optics of the balance sheet and likely produce a more profitable franchise going forward," Citi analyst Benjamin Gerlinger said. First Horizon swung to a loss in the third quarter from a year earlier, as it booked a $473 million loss on the pending mortgage portfolio sale. The bank, which had $84.3 billion in assets as of September 30, plans to partially redeploy proceeds from the mortgage sale into higher-yielding loans in the coming quarters. "We expect the debate to center on how quickly the proceeds are redeployed into higher-yielding commercial loans and whether deposit cost pressure eases enough to support NII as countercyclical fee income softens," Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini said, adding the biggest takeaway from the quarter was the mortgage business realignment. The sale, which is expected to close in the fourth quarter, is anticipated to boost 2027 profit by 4% after tax.

item.title: L’AIE va accélérer la mise sur le marché des stocks de pétrole, dont plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel
item.description: L’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) est convenue jeudi de mettre sur le marché plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible, ainsi que les volumes restants des réserves d’urgence libérées en mars, afin de contribuer à approvisionner le marché et à freiner la flambée des prix.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) est convenue jeudi de mettre sur le marché plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible, ainsi que les volumes restants des réserves d’urgence libérées en mars, afin de contribuer à approvisionner le marché et à freiner la flambée des prix. Le président américain Donald Trump a exhorté les pays de l’Union européenne à puiser dans leurs réserves, menaçant de restreindre les exportations américaines de diesel afin de contenir la hausse des prix avant les élections de mi-mandat du 3 novembre. Les prix du diesel ont atteint des niveaux records sur de nombreux marchés liés à la guerre au Moyen-Orient et au conflit entre la Russie et l’Ukraine, faisant peser des risques inflationnistes et aggravant le coût de la vie pour les gouvernements et les consommateurs. Le conseil d’administration de l’AIE, qui compte 32 pays membres, s’est réuni jeudi pour examiner l’ampleur et le calendrier des mises sur le marché des stocks. "Le conseil de direction de l’AIE a réaffirmé son engagement à poursuivre la mise en œuvre de l’action collective de mars 2026 en réponse à la crise dans le détroit d’Ormuz", a indiqué l’agence dans un communiqué publié à l’issue de la réunion. En mars, les pays membres s’étaient engagés à libérer plus de 400 millions de barils de pétrole brut et de produits pétroliers, alors que les prix s’envolaient. Jeudi, les membres "sont convenus d’accélérer la mise sur le marché des volumes restants, des plans précis étant déjà en place, notamment pour libérer plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible". Le volume de 20 millions de barils de diesel est inférieur aux 50 millions de barils envisagés précédemment, selon une source au fait des discussions. DÉCEPTION FACE À L’ABSENCE DE VOLUMES SUPPLÉMENTAIRES Reuters a rapporté ce mois-ci que les gouvernements de l’Union européenne examinaient une proposition française visant à libérer 50 millions de barils de diesel, auxquels s’ajouteraient 50 millions de barils de pétrole brut provenant des stocks des pays membres de l’AIE. À la suite du communiqué publié jeudi par l’AIE, le contrat de référence européen du gazole, un produit pétrolier comprenant notamment le diesel , a progressé à 1.430,75 dollars (1.277 euros) la tonne à 15h12 GMT, bien qu’il soit resté en baisse sur la séance. "La hausse des prix du gazole laisse penser à une certaine déception face à l’absence d’engagement ferme en faveur de volumes supplémentaires immédiats", a déclaré Ole Hansen, analyste chez Saxo Bank. "Les prix sont élevés, mais nous ne sommes pas confrontés à de véritables pénuries. Dans ce contexte, il est probablement judicieux de conserver nos réserves pour le moment." Selon l'AIE, certains membres ont déjà mis sur le marché des volumes supérieurs à leurs engagements de mars, tandis que d’autres prévoient de faire de même. Environ 330 millions de barils ont été mis sur le marché à ce jour, a précisé l’AIE. Les États-Unis ont indiqué aux autres membres de l’AIE que les plans actuels de libération des réserves ne suffisaient pas à freiner la hausse des prix des carburants, a rapporté jeudi Bloomberg News, citant des sources proches du dossier. La Maison blanche n’a pas répondu dans l'immédiat à une demande de commentaire de Reuters. L’Espagne a annoncé jeudi qu’elle mettrait sur le marché 4,4 millions de barils de ses réserves stratégiques en octobre, sans préciser quels produits seraient concernés. Le pays a jusqu’à présent mis sur le marché 3,7 millions des 11,5 millions de barils qu’il s’était engagé à débloquer en mars.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure
item.description: Yemen's Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray, Mohammed Ghobari, Eman Abouhassira
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict. The attack was the first in the current conflict between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia on Aden's al-Maashiq palace, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government. The conflict is a new theatre in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. The government's prime minister and cabinet members were safe following the attack, Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said. Witnesses told Reuters they heard loud booms near the palace. Yemen's cabinet said the attack involved missiles and drones, and officials told Reuters that two guards were killed. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the Houthis had bombed what he described as the Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden, as part of the group's declared policy of targeting "Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located". The Houthi-run news agency SABA said the headquarters was run by Saudi officers and that there were weapons depots there. Reuters could not independently verify the claims. The renewed fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces resumed in Yemen last month, and aid agencies [USN:L6N4600ML TEXT:"have warned"] of rapidly worsening conditions. Last week, government forces launched a campaign to recapture areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a global shipping artery. Residents of Taiz, northwest of Aden, have said they face [USN:L1N45Z0S1 TEXT:"intensifying bombardment"] and dwindling supplies as the Houthis tighten their grip on areas around the city, Yemen's third-largest. War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when [USN:L1N45Q02Z TEXT:"the Houthis"] seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year. In that phase of the conflict Houthi fighters and allied forces briefly seized al-Maashiq palace during a battle for Aden, before withdrawing. COALITION SAYS HOUTHIS ARE GETTING MISSILES, FAST BOATS As Saudi Arabia backs government forces, the Houthis [USN:L1N4610L5 TEXT:"have been firing"] ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a [USN:L1N46108L TEXT:"pressure point"] in the wider war [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"and threatening"] its ambitious economic plans. On Thursday, the Saudi-led military coalition said the Houthis had attempted to attack dozens of such sites, highlighting the risk to Saudi civilian infrastructure. The governing council of the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization condemned the recent attacks on civilian airports, aircraft, and aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told reporters that the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others. The airport is one of Saudi Arabia's main international aviation hubs. The coalition said Houthi attacks on Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border had killed three people and wounded 28. Maliki said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats. Iran [USN:L1N43P0D6 TEXT:"has provided"] weapons, money and training to the Houthis, although Tehran has officially denied arming them in violation of a UN arms embargo. Maliki also said the coalition had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen's mountainous areas, calling on the Houthis to immediately halt operations targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure. Shortly afterwards, the Houthi military spokesperson said Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, renewing a warning to airlines while excluding airspace over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. Saudi Arabia's civil defence authority also issued an early-warning alert over a potential threat in the southern province of Najran, before saying the danger had passed. Later, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the southwestern Saudi Arabian city of Khamis Mushait, and another launched towards the country's southern region.

item.title: Diálogo sigue estancado en mina chilena Centinela de Antofagasta en huelga: sindicato
item.description: Las negociaciones entre los dos sindicatos en huelga de la mina chilena de cobre Centinela y Antofagasta Minerals continuaban el jueves sin avances, aunque la firma aseguró que esta semana se ha abierto una oportunidad concreta para alcanzar un acuerdo.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Las negociaciones entre los dos sindicatos en huelga de la mina chilena de cobre Centinela y Antofagasta Minerals continuaban el jueves sin avances, aunque la firma aseguró que esta semana se ha abierto una oportunidad concreta para alcanzar un acuerdo. Los gremios Distrito Centinela y Minera Esperanza, con más de 700 socios, iniciaron la paralización el 7 de octubre tras fracasar su negociación contractual, pero volvieron a la mesa de diálogo el martes en un intento por resolver el conflicto. "Hasta el momento, tras tres días de mediación voluntaria, la empresa se ha negado a abordar un mecanismo que ponga término a la discriminación durante la vigencia del contrato colectivo", dijeron los sindicatos en un comunicado. En tanto, tres trabajadores cumplían siete días en huelga de hambre en un intento por presionar una pronta solución al reclamo de los sindicatos de que los trabajadores cuenten con los mismos beneficios independiente del gremio al que estén afiliados. "Tras estimar desproporcionada la medida de protesta (de huelga de hambre), insiste la empresa en informar una oferta económica que fue rechazada por los trabajadores, pero oculta que la real razón del conflicto es la vulneración de los derechos fundamentales de igualdad de trato y no discriminación", agregó. En un comunicado, la empresa aseguró que durante esta semana ha presentado nuevas propuestas con materias relevantes y una mejora significativa en las condiciones económicas. "Esperamos que los socios y las socias puedan evaluar íntegramente las propuestas entregadas y decidir de manera informada. Tenemos la convicción de que el diálogo desarrollado esta semana ha abierto una oportunidad concreta para alcanzar un acuerdo", agregó. Antofagasta (ANTO.L) reiteró que ha logrado sostener su producción en niveles normales "lo que hasta ahora ha evitado los efectos negativos" de la huelga. La compañía reportó el jueves un [USN:L6N4610GA TEXT:"aumento del 7% en su producción del tercer trimestre"] y mantuvo sus previsiones de sumar entre 625.000 y 655.000 toneladas de cobre este año. Centinela produjo unas 240.000 toneladas de cobre en 2025. La huelga en Centinela, además del [USN:L6N4600MP TEXT:"riesgo finalmente no consumado de paralización"] de supervisores en Escondida, de BHP (BHP.AX) , ha dado apoyo a los precios globales del cobre en medio de los temores sobre la dificultad de impulsar la oferta para abastecer el consumo estimado hacia adelante.

item.title: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
item.description: Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Nvidia (NVDA.O) and Apple (AAPL.O) each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project. The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added. The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post. Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, which spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies." "The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," Ingle told Reuters. Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said. Apple declined to comment. The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say it raises questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms. Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term. The planned ballroom is among [USN:L1N3YZ1G0 TEXT:"several projects"] Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab. The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 [USN:S0N42U037 TEXT:"ruling"] in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful." The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure. Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

item.title: Brazilian Camara to replace Ocon at Haas F1 team next season
item.description: Brazilian Rafael Camara will race for Haas next season on a multi-year deal, with the US-owned Formula One team saying on Thursday he was clearly the quickest in a shoot-out test for the seat.
item.dc:creator: Alan Baldwin
item.content:encoded: Brazilian Rafael Camara will race for Haas next season on a multi-year deal, with the US-owned Formula One team saying on Thursday he was clearly the quickest in a shoot-out test for the seat. The 21-year-old Ferrari Academy driver leads the Formula Two standings with two rounds remaining, after winning the F3 title last year. He will be the second Brazilian on the starting grid, with Gabriel Bortoleto already racing for Audi, and plans to take the number 50 since his compatriot races with the 5 that would have been his first choice as a driver born on May 5, 2005. Camara replaces Frenchman Esteban Ocon, whose [USN:L6N45M0IZ TEXT:"departure was announced last month,"] at the Ferrari-powered team. Britain's Oliver Bearman, who also came through the Ferrari Academy, is yet to be confirmed but sure to stay as the more experienced team leader. The signing dashed the immediate hopes of [USN:L4N3YZ0T7 TEXT:"Australian Jack Doohan"], the reserve who had been hoping for a return to a full-time race seat after a [USN:L4N3YE0PV TEXT:"split from Renault-owned Alpine"] last year. "He (Camara) was the quickest, very simple answer. He was impressive," Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu told reporters on a video call when asked what had decided the choice. RESERVE DOOR REMAINS OPEN FOR DOOHAN Komatsu said Doohan's future with the team was "still up in the air" but the door remained open for him to continue in his current role. "We've been talking with him and his manager to see if we can do something together beyond this year," he added. Camara, a former teammate of Mercedes' 20-year-old Formula One championship leader Kimi Antonelli in the FRECA European junior series, showed his pace when he drove last year's Haas in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing in Portugal at the Algarve Circuit in August. "He showed... that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed," said Komatsu. "Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special." The Recife-born Brazilian, who leads Red Bull-backed Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov by seven points in the F2 standings, said his first reaction when Komatsu called to say he had the job was to reply, "Are you sure?" "I'm extremely happy, especially for my parents," he told reporters. "It was a lot of sacrifice on their side. We are not even from the motorsports world, we didn't really know exactly what was the way to go and to be here. "We moved from Recife to Sao Paulo and then eventually they were always travelling with me. So their life, the normal life that they had, they couldn't be doing any more." Camara revealed that his grandmother had raced with a DKW Vemag in the 1960s, but said that was not the reason he had started. Instead the adventure began when the son of a work colleague of his father began karting and his brother then also got the chance but proved reluctant and eventually stopped. "I was always the one that was following and wanting to go but I was still too young, I was five," explained Camara, who has the late triple champion Ayrton Senna as his racing hero. "When I was six I kept asking my dad... and it became something a bit more serious now." Haas are seventh of 11 teams ahead of next week's US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas. Bearman has scored 23 of their 30 points.

item.title: How the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point
item.description: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.
item.dc:creator: Samia Nakhoul
item.content:encoded: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen. By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia's [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"economic ambitions"], they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran's economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources. The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia's prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the [USN:L8N3YO10W TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"] at the mouth of the Gulf to [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb"] in the Red Sea. Iran, under [USN:L6N45K0UX TEXT:"mounting economic"] and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington's strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage. “The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability. [USN:L6N4010N9 TEXT:"The Houthis"] have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends. But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognised government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen. A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"would continue"] unless Saudi restrictions were lifted. The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"could undermine his transformation agenda"], but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030. The Saudi government media office and Iran's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran's behest, saying its demands were centred on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants' salaries from Yemen's own resources. "Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else," he said. FLAGSHIP CONFERENCES DISRUPTED Saudi Arabia has faced a [USN:L6N4600NM TEXT:"widening wave"] of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a [USN:L6N4600QH TEXT:"strike on Saudi Aramco"], the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors. The attacks have disrupted Riyadh's flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives [USN:L6N45Y0GT TEXT:"to withdraw"], and forced organisers to [USN:L6N4600CJ TEXT:"offer remote participation"] at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum. The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire. However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. "They reached a point of NO negotiations," he said. "They have no other choice except military action." The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. "What the Houthis are asking now is a victor's peace," he said. The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington's reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome. SAUDIS HAVE MORE TO LOSE At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS [USN:L6N45308G TEXT:"asked Trump for help"] to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while [USN:L1N45Z0S4 TEXT:"appearing to defer"] any response until after the US midterm elections. The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defences, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favour them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group's advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake. "Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure," he said. "They have so much less to lose than the Saudis." Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis' campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula. At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unravelling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran. "We're heading towards the worst outcome imaginable," al-Muslimi said. "A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies." He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. "The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone," he said. "They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war." (This story has been refiled to remove a no comment reference to the Houthi spokesperson, in paragraph 10.)

item.title: US producer prices post largest gain in 4-1/2 years; expensive gasoline boosts retail sales
item.description: US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising costs for goods and services, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products.
item.dc:creator: Lucia Mutikani
item.content:encoded: US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising costs for goods and services, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. The report from the Labor Department on Thursday also showed fairly large rises last month in key components that go into the calculation of the main inflation measures tracked by the Federal Reserve for its 2% target, leading some economists to still anticipate another interest rate increase this month. Financial markets, however, continued to expect the next rate hike only in December. The government on Wednesday reported a broad increase in [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"consumer prices"] in September. Inflation is being driven by the dragging US-Israeli war with Iran, which is keeping oil prices elevated. Though other data on Thursday showed a stronger-than-expected increase in [USN:L1N460114 TEXT:"retail sales"] last month, that was mostly because consumers paid more for gasoline. The underlying trend in retail sales slowed, consistent with economists' expectations for softer consumer spending growth in the fourth quarter. Inflation is outpacing wages, which have slowed amid tepid hiring, straining finances for consumers, particularly those in the lower part of what economists call a K-shaped economy. "Today's data reinforce a challenging economic crosscurrent: inflation is heating up, the consumer is still spending but with less underlying momentum and the labor market appears frozen rather than broken," said Chris Osmond, chief investment officer at Fifth Third Wealth Advisors. "For the Fed, that is an increasingly uncomfortable combination. A pause remains defensible, but the cost of waiting rises if inflation fails to cool." The Producer Price Index for final demand jumped 1.3% last month, the largest gain since March 2022, after an upwardly revised 0.5% rise in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PPI increasing 0.5% after a previously reported 0.4% gain in August. In the 12 months through September, the PPI soared 6.3%, the biggest rise since December 2022. That followed a 5.6% advance in August. Producer goods prices increased 2.6%, the largest increase since the government started tracking the series in December 2009. A 10.8% surge in energy prices accounted for more than 80% of the broad-based rise in goods prices. Gasoline prices rose 20.3%. Diesel fuel prices increased 21% and soared 115.2% year-on-year. Jet fuel cost more as did residential electric power. Wholesale food prices rebounded 1.2% after declining for three straight months. Food is transported by road and rail, and last month's jump could be an early sign of the effects of record diesel prices spilling over to the broader economy. Fresh and dry vegetable prices vaulted 41.0%, but egg prices dropped 31.9%. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, producer goods prices rose 0.3%. The so-called core goods gained 0.4% in August. Services prices shot up 0.8% after climbing 0.2% in August. A 1.4% surge in margins for trade services accounted for nearly half of the broad-based increase in prices. "The change in margins is an indicator firms are facing higher prices, and could pass those costs on to consumers," said Mark Streiber, economic analyst at FHN Financial. TRANSPORTATION COSTS RISE The cost of transporting freight by road increased 3.8%, while airfares jumped 5.0%, both reflecting higher oil prices. Hotel and motel room prices shot up 5.6%. The cost of legal services rose 0.3%. Airfares, hotel and motel rooms, and legal costs are among the key components that go into the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price indexes. Economists' estimates for the increase in September's core PCE inflation ranged from 0.31% to 0.36%, which could round up to 0.4%. That would translate to a year-over-year rise of 3.1%. Core PCE inflation gained 0.2% in August and advanced 3.0% on a year-over-year basis. Financial markets saw a roughly 30% chance of a rate increase at the Fed's October 27-28 policy meeting, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase were slashed by [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"underwhelming payroll"] gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE [USN:L1N45M0L0 TEXT:"inflation readings"] for July and August. The Fed in September raised its [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"overnight benchmark interest rate"] by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range. Stocks on Wall Street were trading higher. The dollar eased against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields slipped. In a separate report, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said retail sales rose 0.8% in September after jumping 1.3% in August. Economists had forecast retail sales, which are mostly goods and are not adjusted for inflation, gaining 0.3%. Receipts at service stations surged 6.4%. Sales at auto dealerships rose 0.2%. There were also increases in receipts at furniture, electronics and appliance stores as well as online retailers. Sales at food services and drinking places, the only services component in the report, increased 1.1%, which economists tied to spending by higher-income households. Receipts at building material as well as sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and book stores fell. Sales at miscellaneous store retailers dropped 3.0%. Retail sales excluding automobiles, gasoline, building materials and food services edged up 0.1% last month after surging 1.2% in August. These so-called core retail sales correspond most closely with the consumer spending component of gross domestic product. While economists believed consumer spending grew at above a 3.0% annualized rate in the third quarter, they saw the momentum fading by year end. "Higher gas prices are beginning to bite because, unlike earlier in the year, there's no offset this time around from fiscal policy," said Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics. "We expect ... the rise in diesel prices to result in larger price hikes across a broader range of goods and services over the coming months." Growth estimates for the July-September quarter are around a 3.0% rate. The economy grew at a 2.2% pace in the second quarter. A third report from the Labor Department showed [USN:L1N4600ZS TEXT:"initial claims"] for state unemployment benefits rose 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 199,000 last week, still near a 57-year low. "Paychecks may not be keeping up with inflation, but at least people are still getting them," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.

item.title: El Brent cotiza estable mientras EEUU evalúa suavizar sanciones a "flota en la sombra"
item.description: El precio del crudo Brent operaba prácticamente sin cambios el jueves, mientras los inversionistas sopesaban las posibles medidas de Estados Unidos para aliviar las restricciones sobre la "flota en la sombra" de petroleros, y el conflicto en Oriente Medio mantenía una prima de riesgo geopolítico en el mercado.
item.dc:creator: Georgina Mccartney
item.content:encoded: El precio del crudo Brent operaba prácticamente sin cambios el jueves, mientras los inversionistas sopesaban las posibles medidas de Estados Unidos para aliviar las restricciones sobre la "flota en la sombra" de petroleros, y el conflicto en Oriente Medio mantenía una prima de riesgo geopolítico en el mercado. * El Brent subía 2 centavos, o un 0,02%, a 106,08 dólares a las 1614 GMT. Los futuros del crudo West Texas Intermediate (WTI) de Estados Unidos ganaban 2,96 dólares, o un 3,11%, a 98,05 dólares el barril, después de que una importante reducción de las existencias de crudo de Estados Unidos contribuyó a sostener los precios. * Los debates sobre la "flota en la sombra" se producen pocos días después de que el presidente Donald Trump levantó temporalmente las sanciones sobre el diésel ruso para mitigar la subida de los precios a nivel mundial. Las nuevas conversaciones se centran en la posibilidad de que Washington permita que el "petróleo legal" circule en buques anteriormente sancionados, dijo un funcionario estadounidense. * El Departamento de Energía dijo que cualquier medida para aliviar las sanciones sobre la "flota en la sombra" no ayudaría a Rusia a transportar petróleo ni productos petroleros. El Departamento del Tesoro remitió las preguntas al Departamento de Energía. * En tanto, los inventarios de crudo y de destilados de Estados Unidos descendieron, mientras que los de gasolina aumentaron la semana pasada, informó el jueves la Administración de Información de Energía (EIA). * Las existencias de crudo descendieron en 8,6 millones de barriles, a 415,6 millones de barriles, en la semana que finalizó el 9 de octubre, según la EIA, frente a las previsiones de los analistas en una encuesta de Reuters, que apuntaban a una reducción de 288.000 barriles. * La escalada del conflicto entre Arabia Saudita y los hutíes de Yemen, así como los nuevos ataques a buques en la región, respaldaban los precios. Un portacontenedores y un granelero se hundieron cerca del estrecho de Ormuz tras ser alcanzados por proyectiles en incidentes separados, informaron el miércoles fuentes marítimas. * Los ataques en torno a esta vía navegable se han disparado en los últimos diez días, e Irán ha afirmado que está intensificando los ataques en respuesta al bloqueo estadounidense de sus puertos y a las sanciones más severas impuestas el mes pasado. * En tanto, Ucrania reanudó sus ofensivas contra refinerías rusas con un ataque a una planta en la región de Riazán, después de que el presidente ucraniano, Volodímir Zelenski, expresó su indignación por una "peligrosa" retirada de los servicios de inteligencia estadounidenses. * La Agencia Internacional de la Energía acordó el jueves liberar al mercado, lo antes posible, más de 20 millones de barriles de diésel, así como cualquier petróleo restante de la liberación récord de reservas de emergencia prometida en marzo, con el fin de impulsar la oferta y frenar la escalada de los precios.

item.title: Market selloff, rising rates test AI data centre deal boom
item.description: A market selloff is forcing companies driving the global AI boom to delay fundraising plans or pay more for capital as investors demand proof they can absorb rising interest rates and computing-power costs.
item.dc:creator: Yantoultra Ngui, Kane Wu, Clare Jim
item.content:encoded: A [USN:L6N4610C5 TEXT:"market selloff"] is forcing companies driving the global AI boom to delay fundraising plans or pay more for capital as investors demand proof they can absorb rising interest rates and computing-power costs. The shift comes as investors reassess whether the companies racing to build the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence can generate returns that justify soaring spending on computing power, land and energy. In the past week alone, as AI-related stocks have weakened and the debt of data-centre operator [USN:L8N4610AR TEXT:"CoreWeave"] has slumped towards distressed prices, listings for a Blackstone-backed [USN:L4N45Z0H4 TEXT:"AirTrunk"] REIT, Nvidia-backed [USN:L1N45U12T TEXT:"Firmus"] and SoftBank-backed [USN:L6N45H0SG TEXT:"SB Energy"] have either been pulled or paused. The increased scrutiny is not derailing investment in the sector, analysts said, but it is forcing investors to distinguish more sharply between business models and levels of execution risk. "The conversation has shifted from growth at any cost to a much sharper focus on quality," said Harry Evans, a partner at law firm Freshfields. Evans said deal activity could hold up through next year, thanks to a strong pipeline. Recent listing setbacks, however, show investors are becoming more discerning about valuations, leverage and business models. M&A involving Asian data centres is still on track for a record year, reaching $21.3 billion as of Tuesday, according to Dealogic data, more than double the $10 billion recorded in all of 2025. Debt financing has also remained strong, with syndicated loans and bond issuance totalling $22.3 billion so far this year. Equity capital market fundraising for the sector, however, is down, at $5.4 billion so far this year, a 4.6% drop from the same period in 2025. "General thoughts with IPOs are that they often seek 'hype', as they're largely looking for oversubscription," said Nicholas Tuan, director, APAC Advisory Services at real estate services firm Savills. "There may not be fundamental asset value when you peel it all back." Firmus, which had aimed to raise $5 billion in what would have been Australia's second-largest stock market listing, struggled to convince investors it could deliver on ambitious revenue projections while carrying about $30 billion of debt. Nuclear services company [USN:L4N4581N6 TEXT:"Holtec"] cited a "[USN:L4N45H14U TEXT:"perfect storm"]", driven mainly by uncertainty around data-centre demand, when it pulled its US listing last month. HIGHER RATES TEST VALUATIONS Higher borrowing costs are at the heart of the new scrutiny. Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields posted their sharpest quarterly rise this century last month, prompting investors to take a closer look at whether projected revenues can support growing debt burdens, bankers said. Gary Goh, CEO of Sprint DC Consulting, an Asia-Pacific data centre consultancy firm based in Kuala Lumpur, warned higher financing costs could lead to sharp valuation corrections. Valuations can vary widely depending on whether they are based on existing customer contracts or future projections, and whether capital expenditure requirements are fully reflected, said a banker who advises data-centre investors. "There is not remotely enough data centres built for the demand," said the banker, who was not authorised to speak publicly. "Investors are still going in but the question is at what valuation." Investors are also paying closer attention to execution risks. Beyond higher power and water costs, developers face [USN:L1N45M0CN TEXT:"growing opposition"] in some markets over electricity use, noise and environmental concerns, adding to regulatory uncertainty around new projects. Securing suitable land and power supplies is becoming more difficult in some jurisdictions, said a person at a US-based firm that invests in Asian data-centre platforms, adding that the company had tightened its underwriting criteria because of geopolitical and policy risks. To be sure, major transactions are still [USN:L6N460198 TEXT:"moving ahead"]. Singapore-based DayOne is expected to go public as soon as November, seeking to raise up to $5 billion, Reuters [USN:L6N45H0SG TEXT:"reported"] in September. DayOne did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AirTrunk, despite postponing a planned REIT listing, is nearing a deal to sell its Johor data centre in Malaysia to a group of investors including local pension fund KWAP at a valuation of about $1 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter. Bain Capital has also received final bids for at least 40% of its pan-Asian platform Bridge Data Centres in a deal that could value the business at around $5 billion, according to two people with knowledge of the process. AirTrunk's backer Blackstone and Bain Capital declined to comment. KWAP said it was not in a position to comment. Still, investors are likely to differentiate between established wholesale operators with long-term customer commitments and stable revenue, and higher-risk "neoclouds" and "AI-campus builders", said John Dinsdale, chief analyst at TechInsights. "The question for investors is less whether demand will expand than which business models and companies will be best placed to capture that growth sustainably."

item.title: NYC Comptroller Levine urges Anthropic to pause US IPO
item.description: Anthropic should delay its US IPO until it addresses concerns about safety, governance and the pace of development, urged New York City Comptroller Mark Levine in a letter to the AI lab's CEO Dario Amodei.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic should [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"delay its US IPO"] until it addresses concerns about safety, governance and the pace of development, urged New York City Comptroller Mark Levine in a letter to the AI lab's CEO Dario Amodei. AI systems have advanced rapidly over the past 12 months, outpacing regulation and drawing scrutiny over potential risks, including safety, cybersecurity threats and misuse. "Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks," Levine wrote in the letter seen by Reuters on Thursday. NYC's public pension funds have a combined $7 million in exposure to Anthropic through private equity holdings, the comptroller's office told Reuters. Anthropic, which is reportedly targeting a $2 trillion valuation in the listing, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Anthropic's own research has highlighted the risks posed by [USN:L8N45V1NQ TEXT:"increasingly autonomous AI models"], which have demonstrated potentially harmful capabilities in controlled tests, including sabotaging code, facilitating fraud and manipulating information. Earlier this week, in a pre-IPO meeting, Anthropic told prospective investors that revenue in the third quarter surged 45% from the prior quarter, Reuters [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"reported"], citing sources. Its closest rival, ChatGPT maker OpenAI, is expected to list in 2027. New York City's comptroller oversees the city's finances, manages its pension funds and acts as a watchdog over public spending and financial practices. The funds have over $325 billion in assets. The contents of the letter were first reported by CNBC, earlier on Thursday.

item.title: US 10-year Treasury yield levels not unprecedented, BNY CEO says
item.description: The levels the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has touched this year are not unprecedented, the CEO of the oldest US bank told Reuters, as a bruising selloff in government debt lifted yields to multi-decade highs.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Azhar, Arasu Basil, Pritam Biswas
item.content:encoded: The levels the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has touched this year are not unprecedented, the CEO of the oldest US bank (BNY.N) told Reuters, as a [USN:L1N45V0NY TEXT:"bruising selloff in government debt"] lifted yields to multi-decade highs. The 10-year US Treasury yield, a yardstick for global borrowing costs and asset prices, posted its [USN:L8N45N0KW TEXT:"sharpest rise since 1994"] in the July-September period. "We got 10-year rates to like, call it five and a quarter. There's nothing particularly unusual in history about 10-year rates at that level. We've had arguably low levels for a very long time," BNY CEO Robin Vince said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday. "People get very caught up. It has happened quickly, for sure, but with what I would view as more of a normalization of the curve." Global bond markets have come under intense pressure this year as energy prices remain elevated, while the AI boom is supporting economic growth, a combination that has heightened worries about inflation and rising interest rates. "You can make a good case that it is actually the strength of the US economy that's one of the primary drivers of inflation and the move higher in rates," Vince said. Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management, echoed Vince's views. "The bigger adjustment may be psychological. Investors, borrowers and businesses may simply need to get used to these levels. There will be swings along the way, but I would not assume we are going back to the ultra-low-rate world anytime soon," Jacobsen said. AI ROUT The latest hot US inflation report [USN:L6N4600XF TEXT:"sent rate-hike bets soaring"] and deepened investor concerns about the [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"risks posed by rising borrowing costs"] in the capital-intensive AI industry. [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"This week's rout in AI stocks"] eased some pressure on the bond markets, with investors flocking to safe-haven government debt in the face of the tech selloff, pushing US yields down across the curve. The 10-year Treasury yield was [USN:L8N4610QB TEXT:"headed for the largest one-day decline"] since early August 2025 on Thursday. Asked about financial structures in the AI landscape, Vince said on a post-earnings media call on Thursday that over time weak structures will get exposed, and that's the evolution of financial markets and the development of things. DEPOSITS EXPECTED TO PICK UP IN Q4 In a statement, Vince said that client demand is continuing to grow and BNY's sales and pipelines remain very healthy across products and regions. [USN:L1N3I80VH TEXT:"BNY has grown into the world's largest custodian"]. The company sits at the center of global capital markets, safeguarding and administering trillions of dollars in client assets, while processing trades and moving securities and cash between financial institutions. Average deposits are expected to pick up in the fourth quarter along with client activity, Chief Financial Officer Dermot McDonogh told Reuters. BNY on Thursday reported a 20% jump in profit applicable to common shareholders to $1.61 billion in the third quarter, driven by interest income growth and stronger market levels that boosted the value of client assets. Assets under custody and administration rose 10% to $63.4 trillion from a year earlier. The New York-based firm is also benefiting from a rise in interest rates as it reinvests cash from maturing investment securities at higher yields. Net interest income — the spread between earnings from assets and costs on liabilities — accounts for roughly 25% of BNY's revenue, McDonogh said.

item.title: Venture Global inks deals with GE Vernova, Baker Hughes for power expansion
item.description: Venture Global said on Thursday it had signed deals with GE Vernova and Baker Hughes to support up to 16 new power generation units, advancing plans to develop off-grid power capacity that could support AI data centers and its LNG operations.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Venture Global (VG.N) said on Thursday it had signed deals with GE Vernova (GEV.N) and Baker Hughes (BKR.O) to support up to 16 new power generation units, advancing plans to develop off-grid power capacity that could support AI data centers and its LNG operations. The rapid growth of data centers has fueled interest in behind-the-meter power projects as developers seek to secure dedicated electricity supplies without adding strain to already constrained public power grids. Here are more details: The agreements cover up to 16 power-island units of 720 megawatts each, alongside associated transformer equipment Venture said the units could support up to 10 gigawatts of compute capacity by the end of 2034, subject to customer commitments and market demand The company expects to place its first order for a power island by the end of 2026 The gas-fired, combined-cycle units would operate behind-the-meter, without drawing on public power grids or water utilities, the company said Any third-party data center development would be separate from and complementary to its LNG operations and would not affect existing LNG sales commitments, Venture said The company plans to file its first permit applications this week. Additional equipment orders will depend on future commercial and operational requirements This new capacity would expand on the company's 4.5 GW of gas-fired generation that powers its facilities in island mode, allowing the plants to operate independently of the grid

item.title: CoreWeave's slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
item.description: Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave tumbled again on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, laying bare a growing crisis of confidence in an AI build-out increasingly financed with borrowed money.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Anhata Rooprai
item.content:encoded: Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave (CRWV.O) tumbled again on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, laying bare a growing crisis of confidence in an AI build-out increasingly financed with borrowed money. The loss-making AI cloud company is burdened with about $50 billion in debt and has become the poster child for concerns that the data center boom is being fueled by credit, straining newer players and pressuring cash flows even at giants such as Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta Platforms (META.O) . CoreWeave's slump has fueled a global rout in AI stocks, underscoring investor doubts about whether future revenue from the technology can keep pace with the spending. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is CoreWeave's second-largest investor with about a 10% stake, played down the fears. "CoreWeave’s financial strength is improving every day," Huang told reporters at a Stockholm event, adding that he does not see a need for Nvidia to backstop the company. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." CoreWeave stock was last down nearly 2% after slipping as much as 8.3% to its lowest level since May 2025, extending the more than 15% slide from Wednesday and ranking among the biggest decliners in the tech selloff. "The market is waking up to the fact that AI demand and a profitable business model are two very different things," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing. But if the cost of capital keeps rising, even strong demand may not be enough to protect the most heavily leveraged players." The jitters come as [USN:L6N4601DE TEXT:"investors await Anthropic's IPO"], which would be a test of whether the Claude AI model maker's rapid revenue growth can ease worries about runaway AI spending. The market selloff has already led some companies such as [USN:L4N45L0SK TEXT:"smart ring maker Oura"] (OURA.O) to [USN:L4N45V00M TEXT:"push back their listings"]. The yield on CoreWeave's April-issued bonds due 2031 was near 16%, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media. The bond was last down 0.3 cents on the dollar to 79.15 cents, according to Tradeweb data. The [USN:L1N46104Z TEXT:"cost of insuring its debt"] against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, implying a nearly 63% chance of default in five years, up from about 30% a year ago. That is despite a deal under which Nvidia (NVDA.O) will buy any unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 13, 2032. CoreWeave, [USN:L3N3QB14S TEXT:"which went public in March 2025"], leads newer cloud providers known as neoclouds that rent out computing power from scarce and costly Nvidia processors to meet soaring demand, often borrowing heavily to buy the chips. It counts Microsoft and OpenAI among its customers, according to media reports. That leaves neoclouds exposed to any cooling in AI demand, critics have said, while the chips lose value as newer ones arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them. CoreWeave [USN:L4N4481ER TEXT:"raised its annual capital spending forecast"] by $4 billion to as much as $39 billion in August. It is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates. Worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) , a closely watched gauge of chip stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6% slide over the past six sessions. The Nasdaq (.NDX) has declined more than 3% in the period. On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that rising interest rates could hurt the sector. CoreWeave's neocloud rivals Nebius (NBIS.O) , Applied Digital (APLD.O) and Iren (IREN.O) fell between 3% and 7%. In Asia, SoftBank (9984.T) , which has bet heavily on OpenAI, closed down 9.3%. 'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL The CoreWeave selloff came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times that the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital. The same day research firm Gartner said about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030 and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment. "In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030," said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner. "However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period." CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an [USN:L4N4601XL TEXT:"internal memo on Wednesday"] seen by Reuters, telling employees the company's deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally".

item.title: Cobre toca mínimo de casi dos semanas por toma de ganancias, se reducen temores sobre oferta
item.description: Los precios del cobre bajaron a su menor nivel en casi dos semanas el jueves, afectados por una toma de beneficios tras el alivio de las preocupaciones sobre el suministro, una ola de ventas en las acciones del sector de la inteligencia artificial y los temores por el aumento de la inflación y las tasas de interés.
item.dc:creator: Eric Onstad
item.content:encoded: Los precios del cobre bajaron a su menor nivel en casi dos semanas el jueves, afectados por una toma de beneficios tras el alivio de las preocupaciones sobre el suministro, una ola de ventas en las acciones del sector de la inteligencia artificial y los temores por el aumento de la inflación y las tasas de interés. * A las 1625 GMT, el contrato referencial del cobre a tres meses en la Bolsa de Metales de Londres (LME) restó un 1,3%, a 14.298 dólares por tonelada, tras tocar su mínimo desde el 2 de octubre, a 14.256 dólares. * "Están ocurriendo dos cosas al mismo tiempo: el alivio de las preocupaciones sobre el suministro y el fuerte reporte de la inflación", dijo Ole Hansen, responsable de estrategia de materias primas del Saxo Bank en Copenhague. "Eso fue demasiado para que el mercado lo asimilara de golpe y está surgiendo cierta toma de beneficios". * Las perspectivas técnicas también se están deteriorando, con el cobre poniendo a prueba la tendencia alcista iniciada en marzo y algo por debajo de la media móvil de 50 días, añadió. * Los inversores se mostraron menos preocupados por las interrupciones en las explotaciones mineras después de que BHP (BHP.AX) y el sindicato de supervisores de su mina de Escondida, en Chile, anunciaran el miércoles que habían llegado a un acuerdo, evitando así una huelga en la mina de cobre más grande del mundo. * La minera chilena Antofagasta (ANTO.L) comunicó el jueves un aumento del 7% en la producción de cobre del tercer trimestre y mantuvo sus previsiones anuales a pesar de la huelga de los trabajadores sindicados en su mina Centinela. * Una ola de ventas de acciones tecnológicas asiáticas también presionó al mercado de metales. MKTS/GLOB * El contrato de cobre más negociado en la Bolsa de Futuros de Shanghái cayó un 1,9%, a 108.940 yuanes (16.276,46 dólares) por tonelada. * Mientras, el aluminio en la LME avanzó un 0,3%, a 2.995,50 dólares la tonelada, recuperándose después de tocar más temprano su menor nivel en más de nueve meses, en 2.953,50 dólares. * En otros metales básicos, el zinc cayó un 1,1%, a 3.677,50 dólares por tonelada; el plomo perdió un 0,7%, a 1.883 dólares; el níquel restó un 1,7%, a 15.240 dólares; y el estaño cotizó con pocos cambios, a 50.440 dólares, tras alcanzar su nivel más bajo desde junio.

item.title: Northern Ireland's Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in jail for child sex offences
item.description: The former leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party, Jeffrey Donaldson, was sentenced to 15 years in jail on Thursday for child sex offences that were described by the judge as representing "a catastrophic descent into disgrace".
item.dc:creator: Amanda Ferguson
item.content:encoded: The former leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party, Jeffrey Donaldson, was sentenced to 15 years in jail on Thursday for child sex offences that were described by the judge as representing "a catastrophic descent into disgrace". Donaldson [USN:L1N42U0JD TEXT:"was convicted"] in June of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency against two children between 1985 and 2008 in one of the highest-profile cases in the British-run region in recent times. He was one of Northern Ireland's best-known politicians and its longest-serving lawmaker in the British parliament when he was arrested and charged in March 2024. The 63-year-old stared straight ahead as Judge Paul Ramsey handed down the sentence. Ramsey described the case as "disturbing and disquieting" and assessed Donaldson as having a medium chance of reoffending. Donaldson, who has been in prison awaiting sentence since June, denied all charges and is [USN:L8N43J1N7 TEXT:"seeking to appeal"] against his convictions. Prosecution lawyer Rosemary Walsh told a pre-sentencing hearing last month that one of the victims described the abuse as "the worst moment of her life" and that it had affected all her relationships since. The other victim believed her childhood had been stolen and that she had carried around feelings of "shame" ever since. The victims, neither of whom can be identified for legal reasons, gave evidence during the trial. Ramsey said he was in no doubt whatsoever of the permanent mark left on both victims and that this, the length of abuse and age of the victims, were aggravating factors in the severity of the sentence. He said Donaldson had doubled down on his denials and not offered one word of apology or shame.
