item.title: Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
item.description: Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday. Its services gave Israel's Candiru — a spyware company [USN:L1N2RU186 TEXT:"blacklisted by the US government"] — as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google (GOOGL.O) , Comcast (CMCSA.O) , Russia's Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant. The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Discover-Tech's online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said. Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur. Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume. MALICIOUS ADS SHOWN IN HUNDREDS OF SENSITIVE NETWORKS Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned. Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were similarly unsuccessful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for [USN:L1N2RU186 TEXT:"allegedly supplying spyware"] that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics. Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. In a statement, Al Jazeera said it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said. Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads. "You go to almost any site in Palestine — any site — you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said. Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Sandisk (SNDK.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) , and Micron (MU.O) , as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified. In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf. MEASURES AGAINST DISCOVER-TECH TAKEN Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations. Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment. Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been [USN:L6N4240BC TEXT:"targeted using location data"] harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since [USN:L6N44V02G TEXT:"disabled ad tracking"] on some devices.

item.title: Venezuela's Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
item.description: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Thursday to a new US indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Thursday to a new US indictment accusing them of [USN:L6N45U13M TEXT:"conspiring to torture"] political opponents. The additional charges, brought last Thursday, significantly expanded the US criminal case against Maduro, 63, and Flores, 70. They previously pleaded not guilty to charges that they abused their power to [USN:L1N40E0K5 TEXT:"help drug traffickers"] ship cocaine. Maduro and Flores, captured by the US military in a January raid ordered by President Donald Trump and flown to New York, entered their pleas at an arraignment before US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan federal court. They wore tan prison garb and were shackled at the ankles during the hearing. When Hellerstein asked for his plea, Maduro said the accusations had been made previously and were false. "I have seen it in its entirety, Judge Hellerstein," Maduro said, referring to the indictment. "I reject this document in its entirety." The judge cut Maduro off as he spoke and said a plea of not guilty would be entered on his behalf. Flores said, "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty." Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. They would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges. Hellerstein postponed the trial start date by two weeks to June 14, 2027, due to the new charges. 'SQUEEZE THEM HARDER' Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney's office say Maduro directed Venezuelan officials to torture opposition politicians and military personnel accused of plotting against him to maintain power in the South American country. In one alleged incident described in the indictment, Maduro in 2014 directed officials to kidnap military personnel to draw information out of them about possible dissidents, and told officials to "squeeze them harder" when some remained defiant. Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment. Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the United States were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country. Successive US administrations imposed sanctions on top Venezuelan officials and key state companies, citing alleged human rights violations, corruption and election-rigging. Maduro accused the United States of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the South American country's natural resources. CAPTURED AT HOME The pressure campaign culminated in the January 3 raid, when the US military captured Maduro and Flores at their Caracas home and brought them to the United States to face drug trafficking charges announced that same day. Since then, they have been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. Maduro's former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, has led Venezuela since his capture and has ramped up cooperation with the United States. Trump has touted Maduro's capture and the reset of relations with Venezuela as a key foreign policy success heading into the November 3 midterm elections in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.

item.title: UK's Healey says banks are key to economy but keeps tax options open
item.description: British finance minister John Healey said banks were central to the country's economic future on Thursday when pressed by reporters about the likelihood of a windfall tax on their bumper profits in his first budget on October 28.
item.dc:creator: David Milliken
item.content:encoded: British finance minister John Healey said banks were central to the country's economic future on Thursday when pressed by reporters about the likelihood of a windfall tax on their bumper profits in his first budget on October 28. Increasing the 3% surcharge for banks on top of standard corporation tax could raise billions of pounds at a time when many lenders have profited from rising interest rates. However, banks argue they are already highly taxed in Britain compared with some other major financial centres and some analysts say higher bank taxes would see them put up charges. "My observation on the banks is that people too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects," Healey told reporters in Bangkok, where he is attending the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting. "That said, I've got decisions to take in the budget and I will," he added, noting that his comments were not intended to be a steer on any intended tax changes. Following Healey's remarks, the Guardian newspaper reported that it understood the finance minister was [USN:SPN46001Q TEXT:"poised to tax banks"] in his budget. The report said reversing cuts to the bank surcharge would be a possible option considered by Healey, but did not say whether a final decision had been made. MANY BANKING ANALYSTS HAVE PENCILLED IN TAX RISE Analysts covering British banks have in recent weeks suggested an increase in the surcharge that banks pay on their profits is likely, with both a return to the previous 8% level and a smaller rise of 2-3 percentage points seen as options. The surcharge currently raises just over £1 billion ($1.3 billion) a year. However, bank bosses have grown more confident that they will avoid such increases. The chief executives of two British lenders told Reuters in recent weeks they did not expect any increase after arguing that such a tax hike could curb lending. Trade body UK Finance said in response to Healey's comments that an increase in bank taxes "would weaken the UK's competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth". In an interview with Bloomberg Television, Healey described banks as "a part of the jewel ... in the British economic crown". When asked if higher taxes on banks could be offset by lower capital requirements, he said he would not be drawn into budget speculation. UK MAY NEED HIGHER TAXES TO KEEP DEFICIT REDUCTION ON TRACK This week, the IMF singled out Britain for praise among major advanced economies for starting a process of deficit reduction that aims at balancing non-investment spending with tax revenue by the 2029/30 tax year. Previous governments have struggled to meet similar rules, due to economic shocks and setting only medium-term goals. Healey told reporters on Thursday that he intended to "stay the path" on deficit reduction in his first budget, when higher inflation and a global rise in interest rates are likely to narrow the margin he has for hitting his goals. "I've said from day one and week one – and I have (Prime Minister) Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me – I will meet those fiscal rules," he said. "I want the budget to be a budget that gives a bit of breathing space but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans," Healey added. British government borrowing costs last week hit their highest since 1998 and are greater than in any other major advanced economy. ($1 = 0.7545 pounds)

item.title: Cartier-owner Richemont considers joining bidders for De Beers, source says
item.description: Luxury group Richemont , owner of Cartier, is in talks to join a consortium bidding for diamond miner De Beers, which was put up for sale by controlling shareholder Anglo American and is valued at about $1 billion, a person familiar with the matter said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Clara Denina, Olivia Kumwenda-Mtambo
item.content:encoded: Luxury group Richemont (CFR.S) , owner of Cartier, is in talks to join a consortium bidding for diamond miner De Beers, which was put up for sale by controlling shareholder Anglo American (AAL.L) and is valued at about $1 billion, a person familiar with the matter said on Thursday. A deal would give the Swiss luxury goods group greater influence over a core element of its supply chain as natural diamond player De Beers grapples with the rapid ascent of cheaper lab-grown gems. Richemont, which is cash-rich and also owns luxury jeweller Van Cleef & Arpels, is discussing joining the Global Diamond Consortium, a group led by former De Beers CEO Gareth Penny that is vying for Anglo American's 85% stake in the world's most famous diamond miner, the person told Reuters, confirming a Bloomberg News report. Richemont, worth around $113 billion, did not respond to requests for comment. Anglo American declined to comment. Filings show Richemont had around €9 billion ($10.09 billion) in net cash at the end of June, a treasure chest worth several times the entire value of De Beers. "We view Richemont's potential participation as strategically meaningful but more about optics and long-term natural diamond category positioning than a financial event," RBC analysts said in a note. Bloomberg reported that negotiations were advanced, although there was no guarantee Richemont would join the consortium. CONSORTIUM INCLUDES SEVERAL PLAYERS Other investors are lining up. Antwerp, Belgium-based diamond-manufacturing company Pluczenik is also bidding for a stake, the company told Reuters, without disclosing the size of the stake. And US jewellery retailer Signet is in talks to join the consortium, said a source familiar with the company. Signet declined to comment. The company, which owns retail brands including KAY Jewelers, Zales and Jared, has worked with De Beers in recent years on natural diamond marketing campaigns. Shares of Signet were up 3.3% at $111.63 in US trading on Thursday. Any bid for De Beers would also depend on [USN:L8N43J0T4 TEXT:"Botswana's"] government, which owns 15% of the miner and has yet to say whether it intends to exercise a first right of refusal. A spokesperson for Botswana's presidency said on Tuesday that the government would not comment until a transaction had been concluded and signed. Officials said this summer a deal was likely to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026. LONG SEARCH FOR A BUYER Anglo put De Beers [USN:S8N41506W TEXT:"up for sale"] in 2024 as part of a wider restructuring amid falling diamond prices and growing demand for synthetic stones. [USN:S8N41506W TEXT:"De Beers"] has mining and exploration operations in Botswana, Namibia, Angola, South Africa and Canada. Richemont Chairman and controlling shareholder Johann Rupert has affirmed his commitment to natural diamonds in high-end jewellery for his brands, as the industry works to maintain the gems' reputation as a true luxury worth the higher price. Richemont would not be the first high-end jewellery company to directly invest in the mines that produce its diamonds. British diamond brand Graff, for example, holds a 14.9% stake in Gem Diamonds (GEMD.L) , owner of the Letseng mine in Lesotho. 'MONEY PIT' Richemont shares have held up this year and outperformed the struggling luxury sector thanks to strong sales of jewellery, which consumers see as a store of value. Dan Mano, CEO of natural diamond pricing and market advisor Rapaport, said the fact so many parties were involved shows individual groups are reluctant to take a large risk in De Beers. And while Richemont is likely one of its biggest customers, there is a risk the investment becomes "a money pit," RBC analysts said. De Beers has been loss-making since 2023. Last year, it reported an underlying EBIT loss of $787 million on revenue of nearly $3.5 billion. Much depends on whether demand for mined diamonds recovers. Tobias Kormind, managing director and co-founder of jewellery brand 77 Diamonds, said that if the market is at its lowest ebb, De Beers could offer a "completely historic" opportunity. But "if this is not cyclical but structural, the demand does not improve, they waste a lot of money initially, and there's no impact," he added. De Beers CEO Al Cook [USN:S8N41506W TEXT:"told Reuters"] in June that the miner has been steadily cutting its supply of stones to the market and that diamonds would become more rare. He sees higher-quality diamonds increasingly sought after, while the price of lower quality gems remains depressed. ($1 = 0.8924 euros)

item.title: India's top court voids Yes Bank's $880 million AT-1 bond write-off
item.description: India's Supreme Court on Thursday set aside Yes Bank's write-off of 84 billion rupees ($883.70 million) in additional tier-1 bonds, dealing a blow to the lender and regulators that had defended the 2020 wipeout.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi, Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: India's Supreme Court on Thursday set aside Yes Bank's (YESB.NS) write-off of 84 billion rupees ($883.70 million) in additional tier-1 bonds, dealing a blow to the lender and regulators that had defended the 2020 wipeout. Reuters has reviewed a copy of the order. Mid-sized Indian lender Yes Bank, in which Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SUMFDS.UL) now holds a 24% stake, was declared insolvent six years ago. Under a restructuring scheme, new investors were brought in, and its [USN:L4N34523T TEXT:"AT1 bonds were written off"], while equity holders faced only a three-year lock-in on 75% of their shares. AT1 bonds are high-risk debt instruments that offer higher returns but can be written off or converted into equity when a bank comes under financial stress. Yes Bank's AT1 bondholders challenged the write-off, and the Bombay High Court ruled in their favour in 2023. Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India and the federal government appealed that ruling, but the Supreme Court has now upheld the lower court's decision. The Supreme Court said the bank's administrator acted under the "erroneous impression" that he retained the power to write down the bonds after the restructuring scheme was finalised, and ruled that the write-off was "impermissible". "We have good reasons to infer that the central government had taken a conscious decision to exclude the clause permitting writing down of the AT-1 Bonds from the Reconstruction Scheme," the top court said. Yes Bank shares fell as much as 14.5% after the ruling. The lender said in an exchange filing it was "in the process of obtaining and examining the final order copy of the judgment." Restoring the AT1 bonds would result in a one-time hit to Yes Bank's profit and loss account and reduce its capital adequacy ratio. "This decision creates regulatory uncertainty that can have the potential to impact investor sentiment," said Vivek Ramji Iyer, a partner and national leader for the financial services risk advisory practice at Grant Thornton. Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation bought a 24.99% stake in the Mumbai-based lender last year. RELIEF FOR BOND HOLDERS The ruling is a relief for Yes Bank's AT1 bondholders, who had argued the securities were mis-sold and could not be written off after the restructuring plan was finalised. "We now urge the bank to return our money without further delay so we can close this chapter," said Saurabh Mehta, a Bengaluru-based retail investor whose parents hold the bonds. The Supreme Court said Yes Bank had sold the bonds to individual investors in breach of RBI rules restricting such high-risk securities to institutions including mutual funds and insurers. The bank "not only permitted but actively offered" the bonds to individuals, it said. "A tighter scrutiny ought to have been exercised before luring individual investors to such high-risk securities," the court said. The court also said the RBI was "a mere bystander" as Yes Bank's core equity capital ratio fell to 0.6% by the end of 2019, against a required 7.375%. Institutional investors including Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund and Nippon India Asset Management, which held the securities, also stand to benefit from the ruling. Kotak and Nippon, however, temporarily halted subscriptions to some funds that held the bonds, citing the prospect of a sudden increase in their net asset values, which could sharply raise the price of units for new investors. ($1 = 95.0550 Indian rupees)

item.title: Cohere moves to buy AI cybersecurity startup Aisle
item.description: Canadian AI lab Cohere said on Thursday it had signed a letter of intent to buy Aisle, a San Francisco-based cybersecurity startup that uses AI to detect vulnerabilities in software.
item.dc:creator: Leo Marchandon
item.content:encoded: Canadian AI lab Cohere said on Thursday it had signed a letter of intent to buy Aisle, a San Francisco-based cybersecurity startup that uses AI to detect vulnerabilities in software. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. The tie-up would add cybersecurity to the business entity Cohere is assembling through its [USN:L6N4580NZ TEXT:"merger with Germany's Aleph Alpha"], a combination reported to be worth about $20 billion. It would also extend its European footprint with Aisle's engineering hub in Prague. Cohere said the acquisition reflected its continued investment in Europe and would deepen its presence across the region, strengthening European AI. The deal is aimed at boosting the combined group's security and threat detection capabilities for enterprise and public sector clients, with private deployment available on the customer's own system. "Increasingly capable AI systems are transforming both cybersecurity and the threats organizations face, and defensive capabilities must advance just as quickly," Cohere said. Aisle was founded in 2025 by Ondrej Vlcek, former CEO of Czech antivirus maker Avast, with co-founders from Google (GOOGL.O) DeepMind and Anthropic. Vlcek will join Cohere to lead its new cybersecurity unit, while Aisle Chief Operating Officer Jaya Baloo will become its chief information security officer and Aisle's 50 full-time employees will join Cohere, the Canadian company told Reuters. Aisle said its AI found more than 500 new bugs in widely used software in its first year, including 12 vulnerabilities in OpenSSL, a free program that encrypts internet traffic for banks, governments and messaging apps. The bugs were fixed after their discovery.

item.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq pare declines as AI rout teeters; healthcare, staples gain
item.description: The S&P 500 recouped most of its early losses to trade near flat on Thursday as a selloff in AI stocks eased and investors rotated into defensive sectors as fresh data pointed to building US price pressures.
item.dc:creator: Sruthi Shankar, Purvi Agarwal
item.content:encoded: The S&P 500 recouped most of its early losses to trade near flat on Thursday as a selloff in AI stocks eased and investors rotated into defensive sectors as fresh data pointed to building US price pressures. The Nasdaq neared a one-month low earlier in the session as tech stocks lost ground after TSMC (2330.TW) struck [USN:L1N461004 TEXT:"a cautious note"] on 2027. Reports of a 45% sequential jump in [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"Anthropic's"] quarterly revenue offered little reprieve. By the afternoon, most stocks recovered from declines on Thursday. Cloud computing giant Oracle reversed course to gain 2.1%. The S&P 500 information technology (.SPLRCT) sector lost 1.1%, with gains in software stocks and tech heavyweights such as Microsoft (MSFT.O) cushioning the fall. Chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA.O) was down 1.9% and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O) lost 4%. The broader Philadelphia semiconductor index (.SOX) fell 2.4%, putting it on track for a seventh straight decline and nearly $2 trillion in combined market-value losses in the period. On the flip side, traditionally defensive sectors continued to rise, with healthcare (.SPXHC) and consumer staples (.SPLRCS) adding 2.6% and 1%, respectively. Drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) gained 5.2%, UnitedHealth (UNH.N) was up 4%, while Walmart rose 2.3% after a rating upgrade by Deutsche Bank. "That is emblematic of a defensive rotation. It's because of the worry that maybe some sort of a debt crisis is emerging," said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. Still, heavily indebted data-center operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) lost 1.3% after a 15% drop on Wednesday. Its bonds also fell, pushing yields to record highs. "There has been growing concern about the cash flow reality underlying the AI narrative and has been building at a time that rates have been rising and (interest) rate volatility is increasing," said Jordan Rizzuto, CIO at GammaRoad Capital Partners. "To the degree that rate volatility persists, we would expect credit related pressures to continue to mount for such (indebted) companies." At 12:44 p.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 457.99 points, or 0.89%, to 52,078.61, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 3.74 points, or 0.05%, to 7,722.68, and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 126.38 points, or 0.47%, to 26,566.48. The CBOE Volatility Index (.VIX) , considered Wall Street's fear gauge, hit a two-week high on Thursday and was swinging between gains and losses. Data showed US producer prices [USN:L1N460127 TEXT:"increased by the most"] in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. Markets will now scrutinize Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech before the International Monetary Fund Annual Meeting. [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"Hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data"] on Wednesday had fueled expectations of further interest-rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, after which the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq marked their biggest one-day fall since July. Shares of [USN:L4N46023Y TEXT:"Rocket Lab"] (RKLB.O) dropped 10.9% after the space company said the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year. FMC (FMC.N) slid over 31% after the agrichemicals company [USN:L4N46114X TEXT:"sharply cut"] its third-quarter outlook, which includes a $625 million-$675 million hit from commercial actions. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.34-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.52-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 23 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 351 new lows.

item.title: PepsiCo warns 'energy drink' ban could run its India supplies dry as Red Bull sells on
item.description: PepsiCo told an Indian court on Thursday that a continued ban on the "energy drink" label could drive its top-selling products out of stock nationwide in two months, though rival Red Bull is free to sell its own products for now.
item.dc:creator: Munsif Vengattil
item.content:encoded: PepsiCo (PEP.O) told an Indian court on Thursday that a continued ban on the "energy drink" label could drive its top-selling products out of stock nationwide in two months, though rival Red Bull is free to sell its own products for now. The remarks came as the Delhi High Court again refused to let PepsiCo resume making drinks carrying the prized label, barred by the regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). "There will be no goods in the market after a couple of months," PepsiCo's lawyer, Sandeep Sethi, told the court. "My competitors are able to manufacture." Red Bull won a court [USN:FWN45K14D TEXT:"reprieve"] last month from the regulator's order, but rivals PepsiCo, Monster (MNST.O) and Reliance Consumer have so far been limited to selling [USN:L1N45S03Z TEXT:"existing stocks"] bearing the label. The case is a test of how far the food safety regulator can go in policing product labels in India's rapidly growing energy-drink market, built largely on PepsiCo's . In June, the regulator ordered makers of high-caffeine drinks to drop the term "energy drink", amid growing concerns about the health risk of such products. 'HAVOC IN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM' Energy drinks boomed in India after PepsiCo launched Sting in 2017, with its 20-rupee ($0.21) plastic bottles proving popular among 15- to 19-year-olds and in rural areas, Euromonitor says. PepsiCo also sells its energy drink Adrenaline Rush in the market. Starting over was "a long cumbersome process", Sethi told the court, with the company's cans already bought and printed. "That will play havoc with our entire distribution system," he added. The court has yet to rule on the merits of the ban, with the next hearing in the case set for October 30.

item.title: European shares hit more than two-week high as sturdy earnings lift sentiment
item.description: European shares hit their highest in more than two weeks on Thursday, helped by solid earnings and a surge in healthcare stocks which have emerged as a refuge for global investors when the AI trade fades.
item.dc:creator: Avinash P, Niket Nishant
item.content:encoded: European shares hit their highest in more than two weeks on Thursday, helped by solid earnings and a surge in healthcare stocks which have emerged as a refuge for global investors when the AI trade fades. Shares of Ericsson (ERICb.ST) rose 6.8% and were the top gainer on the benchmark after the Swedish telecom gear maker reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. Investors have pinned their hopes on a robust earnings season to pull the STOXX 600 out of the narrow range it has been confined to over the past month. On Thursday, the pan-European STOXX 600 index (.STOXX) rose 0.38% to 640.16 points after hitting its highest since September 30 earlier in the session. The healthcare index (.SXDP) rose 2.4% and was among the top gainers on the benchmark. Technology shares (.SX8P) lost 1.5% and led declines, dragged down by German chip systems manufacturer Aixtron's (AIXGn.DE) 13% drop. Chip stocks Infineon (IFXGn.DE) and Soitec (SOIT.PA) fell 5.2% and 7.7%, respectively, while chip equipment maker ASML (ASML.AS) dropped 4.2%. Tech stocks across the globe were rattled after [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"hot US inflation data"] on Wednesday stoked fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes, hitting companies that rely on debt to fund AI infrastructure build-outs. "The CPI pressure is still with us and that is triggering some more fear on long-duration stocks, for techs, and also on their financing," Michele Morganti, senior equity strategist at Generali Investments, said. Mondi (MNDI.L) tumbled 7.9% after the paper and packaging firm said [USN:L6N4610G0 TEXT:"it raised prices"] for several paper grades in the third quarter to offset energy and raw material costs. Antofagasta (ANTO.L) slid 4.1% after the miner reported copper production of 436,900 tons year to date, [USN:L1N46106S TEXT:"down 8.3%"] from the same period in 2025. The drop, along with weaker copper prices, pulled the mining sector (.SXPP) down 0.8%. Separately, data showed that consumer prices in France rose 3.4% year-on-year in September on an EU-harmonised basis, in line with a preliminary reading from late September. Traders see an 87% chance that the European Central Bank will deliver a quarter-point rate hike in December, according to LSEG data, after it raised rates twice earlier this year to tackle inflation driven by higher energy prices. "The inflation rates in Europe are reflective of energy problems and industrial bottlenecks. When you have these kinds of problems, you actually need more capital in the system to try to address some of them," said James Rasteh, co-founder and chief investment officer at Coast Capital Management. The World Economic Forum [USN:L6N4610XU TEXT:"could appoint"] Christine Lagarde as its next chair as soon as next month, four people close to the organisation told Reuters, meaning she would step down early as ECB chief and trigger a wider reshuffle at the top of the central bank.

item.title: Apollo's easyJet buyout faces union pushback ahead of first quarter 2027 close
item.description: EasyJet faces opposition from unions over its £5.7 billion ($7.5 billion) takeover by Apollo , though the airline says it remains on track to complete the deal before the end of the first quarter of next year.
item.dc:creator: Yamini Kalia, Gianluca Lo Nostro
item.content:encoded: EasyJet (EZJ.L) faces opposition from unions over its £5.7 billion ($7.5 billion) [USN:L4N4431HA TEXT:"takeover"] by Apollo (APO.N) , though the airline says it remains on track to complete the deal before the end of the first quarter of next year. In a scheme document published on Thursday, easyJet said unions across Europe had raised concerns about the airline's ownership structure after the takeover, with the European Works Council opposing the deal. "The EWC considers that the transaction, as structured, is likely to weaken easyJet's long-term resilience and to expose employees across Europe to risks that are neither addressed nor mitigated by the assurances given," the council said in the document. The EWC also said the deal provided employees with only 12 months of non-binding commitments. Employee representative bodies in France, Portugal and Spain also stopped short of endorsing the acquisition, while others in Britain and Germany adopted a neutral position on its financial terms. EasyJet said it had secured some regulatory approvals in Austria, Britain, France, Germany and Malta, although additional clearances remain outstanding in those countries as well as other jurisdictions. EasyJet's shares were up 1.2% at 0755 GMT. OWNERSHIP SCRUTINY The document comes as easyJet and Apollo seek to reassure aviation regulators about the carrier's ownership structure, a key hurdle for a deal that could set a precedent for private-equity takeovers of Europe's tightly regulated airlines. Apollo has sought to address those concerns through a governance framework designed to ensure easyJet remains majority-controlled by European interests. The private-equity firm's strategy centres on expanding easyJet beyond its traditional no frills model, with plans for a new loyalty programme, premium travel products and additional revenue streams aimed at boosting customer spending. EasyJet plans to hold court and shareholder meetings in the week starting November 9 to approve the deal, formally launching the court-sanctioned process that could remove the airline from the London stock market after more than 25 years. ($1 = 0.7557 pounds)

item.title: Is the AI rout making bonds safe again?
item.description: A rude awakening over the debt-fuelled AI binge has sent investors rushing out of stocks and into government bonds, which now seem to be reclaiming their status as a safe haven and a hedge against equity and credit market wobbles.
item.dc:creator: Ankur Banerjee, Tom Westbrook
item.content:encoded: A [USN:L6N45Z12J TEXT:"rude awakening"] over the debt-fuelled AI binge has sent investors rushing out of [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"stocks"] and into government bonds, which now seem to be reclaiming their status as a safe haven and a hedge against equity and credit market wobbles. For much of the year, bonds have offered little protection as inflationary pressure pushed borrowing costs to multi-decade highs, leaving investors warily looking to hedge funds and other assets as alternatives. But on Wednesday, something strange happened: Treasuries and other government bonds rallied sharply, despite a hotter-than-expected US inflation report, which left chances of a US rate hike from the Federal Reserve this year on the table. The bigger concern for investors now is whether massive AI spending will pay off soon enough, especially with inflation running hot, and how much longer companies will be able to continue to raise funds at current costs of capital. Credit markets are also showing strain, with the cost of insuring some AI-exposed companies against default [USN:L4N4610DV TEXT:"hitting"] records. "The upside surprise in US CPI and the subsequent rally in bonds is highly counter-intuitive," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities. "The cleanest read through is that the slump in AI is repricing growth expectations down leading to bonds serving as a hedge for stocks," he said. On Thursday, the yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 8.4 basis points to 5.105%, hitting its lowest level in three weeks and easing away from the 24-year high it touched last week. The benchmark 10-year JGB yield dropped 6.5 bps to 2.93%, the lowest since September 10. Futures for German bunds and French OATs were up 0.7% Wagers on a near-term move were also tempered after San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said further hikes would probably be needed but signalled no need to act at the October 27-28 meeting. AI TRADE UNWINDS The question left for investors, who remain unsettled by high volatility for rates, is whether an asset that's been dragged by soaring sovereign debt and hot inflation is capable of offering a cushion if equities start to take a bigger tumble. Treasury yields posted their sharpest quarterly rise since 1994 in the July-September period. "Bond-equity correlation is definitely fracturing," said Damien Boey, portfolio strategist at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney. "Usually, growth stocks do well in particular when bond yields fall, but last night growth stocks doing badly drove a safe-haven bid for bonds and their yields lower." Earlier this week, BlackRock Investment Institute [USN:L1N45Z07S TEXT:"downgraded"] its view on US stocks to neutral, citing volatility around AI, and upgraded Treasuries, preferring short-term notes. The rout has been building for days as investors get increasingly nervous about AI spending. The selloff in global equities centred on AI stocks that have powered the markets to record highs in recent years. South Korea's KOSPI (.KS11) , an epicentre of the AI boom, sank 8%, set for its seventh straight decline. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index (.SOX) dropped 4.3% on Wednesday, down for a sixth straight session, its longest losing streak since May 2025. "Investors are separating AI companies with deep cash flows from those that need debt to build," said Kenneth Goh, UOB Kay Hian's director of private wealth management. "Private credit is where it could spread next," Goh said. "Listed lenders to tech and venture companies already trade at steep discounts to their asset values, and more cautious lenders can slow the AI build-out well before any defaults appear." Selling this week has been particularly intense in data centre operator [USN:L4N4601XL TEXT:"CoreWeave"] (CRWV.O) , which has issued $22 billion of bonds and $26 billion of loans, according to LSEG data. "Much of the spending is by companies borrowing to rent computing power to AI labs that don't yet earn enough to cover the bill," said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager at Minotaur Capital. "When CoreWeave's bonds yield 15%, investors are asking whether the end customers will make enough money to keep paying in three or four years," she said.

item.title: AI credit worries send default insurance to record high
item.description: The cost of insuring against tech defaults struck record highs on Thursday, as investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade, with heavily indebted data centre operators like CoreWeave hit hardest.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: The cost of insuring against tech defaults struck record highs on Thursday, as investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade, with heavily indebted data centre operators like CoreWeave (CRWV.O) hit hardest. Hotter-than-expected [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US inflation data"], together with mounting expectations for higher interest rates, are adding to concerns about how quickly massive investment in artificial intelligence will translate into profits, as well as whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Credit default swaps (CDS) are sending a warning signal to markets. The standouts were five-year CDS spreads for CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , which blew past 1,100 bps, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data , while the yield on the company's 2031 bond rose to as much as 16% before retreating to around 14%. Cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) , which has also stirred up investor angst because of its vast borrowing, saw its CDS near 300 bps, bringing the rise this week to around 31 bps. CDS for Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Franco-Italian chipmaker STMicroelectronics and SpaceX (SPCX.O) , which offers some AI services, rose sharply. CoreWeave, a loss-making "neocloud" company that owes nearly $50 billion, according to LSEG data, is in the eye of the storm. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade’s canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "Its bonds have sold off sharply ... this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions." A surge in quarterly revenue from [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"AI developer Anthropic"] did little to calm the market's nerves. According to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with the company's leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday, third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $2 trillion. DEBT MARKET JITTERS CDS spreads show the number of basis points charged for default protection. The greater the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread, meaning the 1,000 bps for CoreWeave CDS implies a risk of default in the coming five years of 64%, up from around 30% a year ago. Earlier this week, [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"Broadcom Chief Executive"] Hock Tan compared the investor rush for anything AI-related to "casino gambling." CoreWeave stock was down another 2% on Thursday, following a 15% slide on Wednesday, meaning nearly a fifth of the company's value has burned up in two days. CoreWeave shares have now fallen 10% since the start of this year, while those of rival Nebius (NBIS.O) , for which there are no publicly tradable CDS, are up about 114%. Credit default swap spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta (META.O) also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave. "This is not the first time we’ve had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action. AI financing costs aren’t dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.

item.title: Global financial watchdog calls for more human oversight of agentic AI
item.description: The Financial Stability Board (FSB), a global standard setter, has called for greater human oversight of agentic AI in final guidance for banks and other firms on managing the technology's risks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Financial Stability Board (FSB), a global standard setter, has called for greater human oversight of agentic AI in final guidance for banks and other firms on managing the technology's risks. The FSB's guidance, published Thursday, comes as regulators ramp up efforts to contain growing AI risks including the threat of AI-enabled cyber attacks, Reuters [USN:L6N45Z0FI TEXT:"reported"] this week. In draft guidance published in June, which it [USN:L6N42H10F TEXT:""strongly encouraged" boards to refer to,"] the FSB warned that AI agents - which can plan and execute tasks with limited human oversight - pose distinct challenges for human oversight Publishing its final guidance, the group said it had strengthened its recommendations on agentic AI, citing feedback on the draft, growing interest among financial institutions in adopting the technology, and the distinct risks and controls it entails A series of incidents has heightened policymakers' concerns about the potential for AI systems to circumvent safeguards, including an incident in July in which an OpenAI agent escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked AI company Hugging Face Among the changes, the FSB now says that in higher-risk use cases, more intensive human oversight will be critical Firms should set clear, risk-based triggers for when an agent must seek human approval, it added The FSB has also removed a guideline that said financial institutions should treat AI as "synthetic employees". Instead, firms should recognise that "AI agents do not reason like humans and may interpret pre-defined goals in unexpected ways."

item.title: Gold rebounds on weaker dollar, yield drop; October Fed hike bets subdued
item.description: Gold climbed more than 1% on Thursday, looking set to snap three sessions of losses, supported by a weaker dollar and lower US Treasury yields, while expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month remained subdued despite hotter-than-expected inflation data.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sinha
item.content:encoded: Gold climbed more than 1% on Thursday, looking set to snap three sessions of losses, supported by a weaker dollar and lower US Treasury yields, while expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike this month remained subdued despite hotter-than-expected inflation data. Spot gold was up 1.1% at $4,149 per ounce by 12:36 a.m. EDT (1636 GMT), after slipping to a one-week low in the previous session. US gold futures for December delivery rose 1.5% to $4,170.10 per ounce. The dollar (.DXY) slipped 0.4%, while the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield were at a three-week low. "I think the market was largely anticipating the hot PPI print in the wake of yesterday's higher than expected CPI number," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals. "The market is starting to realize that the Fed is hamstrung to some degree because of the fiscal situation and that raising interest rates much higher is going to be quite a burden to the economy." Higher interest rates make the non-yielding asset less attractive. US [USN:L1N460127 TEXT:"producer prices increased"] by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising costs for goods and services, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. The data followed Wednesday's consumer price report, which showed [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"prices"] accelerated in September on a surge in gasoline costs. Market pricing for an October Fed rate hike rose sharply after the CPI data. However, San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N4601E8 TEXT:"Mary Daly"] and Vice Chair for Supervision [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"Michelle Bowman"] underscored that an immediate rate hike might not be required, tempering expectations of an October rate hike. Traders are now pricing in about a 29% chance of a rate hike later this month, according to CME's FedWatch Tool . Investors are also looking out for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's comments at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting at 11:30 p.m. EDT for any clues ahead of this month's Fed meeting. Among other metals, spot silver gained 2.3% to $56.90 per ounce, platinum rose 0.4% to $1,613.75 per ounce and palladium climbed 3.2% to $1,129.20 per ounce.

item.title: Brent steady as US weighs easing sanctions on global 'shadow fleet'
item.description: Brent crude was little changed on Thursday as investors weighed possible US steps to ease restrictions on the world’s "shadow fleet" of tankers, while conflict in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market.
item.dc:creator: Georgina Mccartney
item.content:encoded: Brent crude was little changed on Thursday as investors weighed possible US steps to ease restrictions on the world’s "shadow fleet" of tankers, while conflict in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market. The international benchmark was up 2 cents, or 0.02%, at $106.08 at 12:14 p.m. EDT (1614GMT) US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up $2.96, or 3.11%, to $98.05 a barrel, after a large US crude stock draw helped support prices. The shadow fleet discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"temporarily lifted sanctions"] on Russian diesel fuel to ease a surge in prices globally. The new talks centre on Washington potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, [USN:L1N46017R TEXT:"a US official said"]. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help [USN:L1N46017R TEXT:"Russia "]move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy. Meanwhile, US crude stocks and distillate inventories fell while gasoline inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. Crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 288,000-barrel draw. SHIP ATTACKS SUSTAIN OIL RISK PREMIUM Escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis and renewed attacks on ships in the region supported prices. A [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank"] near the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. "The ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is keeping a geopolitical premium in oil markets, but energy infrastructure has not been attacked in the last several days," MUFG analysts said in a note. Meanwhile, [USN:L6N4610BB TEXT:"Ukraine resumed its attacks"] on Russian refineries with a strike on a plant in the Ryazan region, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy voiced anger at a "dangerous" withdrawal of US intelligence. The International Energy Agency [USN:L1N4610MY TEXT:"agreed "]on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market as soon as possible and any oil remaining from a record emergency reserves release pledged in March to boost supply and cool soaring prices. In March, countries had pledged to release more than 400 million barrels of crude and oil products as prices soared. Spain will [USN:L6N4610OA TEXT:"release"] 4.4 million barrels from strategic reserves in October, an Energy Ministry official said on Thursday.

item.title: Global stocks edge lower as AI and rate fears hit tech
item.description: Global equity markets edged lower on Thursday as concerns about AI spending and higher interest rates fueled a continued selloff in technology and chip stocks.
item.dc:creator: Chibuike Oguh
item.content:encoded: Global equity markets edged lower on Thursday as concerns about AI spending and higher interest rates fueled a continued selloff in technology and chip stocks. Investors have been unnerved by valuations of companies in the AI ecosystem as more voices question the sustainability of demand for data centers. On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down while the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index (.SOX) was last down 2%. The benchmark S&P 500 reversed losses in early trade and was trading higher led by healthcare and materials stocks while the Dow was up 1%. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , a heavily indebted data-centre operator in the eye of the recent AI storm, fell another 1.8% following a 15% drop on Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 1.07%, the S&P 500 (.SPX) rose 0.16%, and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 0.23%. A brutal tech-led selloff had hit stocks in Asia. South Korea's KOSPI index (.KS11) , whose flock of top chipmakers made it one of the main beneficiaries of AI euphoria, plunged almost 8%, while the Nikkei 225 (.N225) fell nearly 5%. "I think the selloff reflects investor caution towards the more vulnerable segment of the AI ecosystem, with tech chiefs advocating a slower pace of frontier model development," said Rong Ren Goh, portfolio manager at Eastspring Investments. "Markets increasingly question the sustainability and trajectory of demand for computing capacity. These concerns are compounded by higher funding costs, which raises the investment hurdle rates of capital intensive AI infrastructure projects." MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) closed 3.04% lower, marking its biggest one-day drop since late July. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) fell 0.19%. European stocks (.STOXX) erased early-session losses and finished up 0.33%. BOND YIELDS FALL Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell back towards 5% in what was their biggest daily drop in more than a year. US producer prices rose by the most in 4-1/2 years in September as goods and services costs increased, suggesting that inflation pressures are spreading beyond energy. New US [USN:L1N460114 TEXT:"retail sales data"] showed they increased more than expected last month, boosted by higher gasoline prices, but they also pointed to spending elsewhere remaining moderate. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 10.29 basis points to 5.087%. DOLLAR DROPS Wednesday's [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US inflation data"] had once again tweaked expectations for the Fed's rate path, with traders briefly pricing in roughly even odds of a hike this month, before scaling back those bets. Fed funds futures are now pricing an implied 73% probability the US central bank will stay on hold at the end of its next two-day meeting on October 28, little changed from the start of the week, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. In the currency markets, the dollar slipped from an 18-month peak. Against the yen it was down 0.1% at 158.14 yen, while the euro was up 0.42% at $1.12 and sterling was 0.45% higher and buying $1.33. In [USN:L1N46101K TEXT:"oil markets"], Brent crude reversed losses and was up 0.2% at $106.35 a barrel as traders weighed up the effects of US sanctions relief on supply against attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Spot gold rose 1.23% to $4,155.78 an ounce.

item.title: AI rout slows as investors buy the dip on tech
item.description: A market rout centering on the riskiest AI-related borrowers moderated on Thursday, with buyers returning to the tech sector following a weak US open and as a decline in bond yields eased pressure on the sector.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak, Darshan R, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: A market rout centering on the riskiest AI-related borrowers moderated on Thursday, with buyers returning to the tech sector following a weak US open and as a decline in bond yields eased pressure on the sector. In the spotlight once more was data center operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , which was down 2% at midday after falling as much as 10% earlier on Thursday and [USN:L4N4601KQ TEXT:"tumbling 15% on Wednesday"]. The company's bonds traded at yields as high as 16% and its credit default swap spreads [USN:L1N46104Z TEXT:"widened,"] the latest sign of distress centering on rising financing costs. Wednesday's [USN:L6N4600XF TEXT:"hot US inflation report"] crystallized risks posed by rising borrowing costs in the capital-intensive AI sector. Renewed selling focused on large borrowers such as AI infrastructure provider Nebius (NBIS.O) , off 5%, and big market gainers this year, such as AI server seller Dell Technologies (DELL.N) , down 7%, and memory chipmaker Sandisk (SNDK.O) , down 2%. For the year, Nebius is up 112%, Dell is up 273% and Sandisk is up 476%, LSEG data show. Some investors said an infrastructure buildout billed as the largest ever was inevitably going to have ups and downs, and more volatility was likely, given increasing interest rates and expectations of further Federal Reserve policy tightening. “While increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer for the Americas and global head of equities in the UBS Chief Investment Office. AI SLOWDOWN CONCERNS Some investors said the concerns about CoreWeave and similarly situated players stemmed in part from the perception that business is slowing at Anthropic and OpenAI, the two large AI labs at the center of the boom. According to an investor who attended a meeting with Anthropic's leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday, third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter. Some analysts said that figure was disappointing given expectations for the sector and that Anthropic is targeting a $2 trillion valuation. "We're getting a whole lot of information suggesting that the largest AI companies may not be generating the earnings or revenue people anticipated, and I think that makes everyone nervous about companies like CoreWeave," said Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said in an internal memo the market is acting “irrationally” and that he remains confident in the AI cloud company, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. Investors generally remain sanguine on the sector in part because its largest players, from chip designer Nvidia (NVDA.O) to the [USN:L4N45T0NO TEXT:"hyperscalers"] — primarily Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) , Meta (META.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) — are highly profitable and widely perceived as well managed, despite concerns about debt. But higher rates will make borrowing and building costlier, a fact that is likely to hit unprofitable and less-profitable firms first. On Thursday, US interest rates extended their recent declines, with the 10-year Treasury yield briefly flirting with 5% before resuming its ascent, but high inflation has changed investor expectations. "I do think long rates above 5% and creeping towards 6% is a problem for the marginal borrower, I'll call them," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird. "It gets a lot harder for the tiers below the kind of big four hyperscalers." The Nasdaq (.IXIC) was down 0.4% on Thursday afternoon, with Alphabet and the other hyperscalers mostly little changed. SpaceX (SPCX.O) , another major AI player, was down 3%. "This select group of companies is driving most of the growth in the economy and the stock market, and they're investing so, so aggressively and investors just aren't really willing to pay for it or fully buy in to the extent that we saw in the late 90s or whatever when investors kind of lost their minds," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. "Investors have definitely not lost their minds. They're being very cautious, and I think selective."

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe finit dans le vert, la baisse des rendements compense la débâcle de la "tech" 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bourses européennes ont terminé en hausse jeudi, profitant de la forte baisse des rendements obligataires dans un contexte de ventes massives dans le secteur technologique, qui est à nouveau l'objet de la méfiance du marché en raison de son niveau d'endettement élevé. Christine Lagarde pourrait être nommée présidente du Forum de Davos dès novembre-sources ZURICH/BANGKOK, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le Forum économique mondial (WEF) pourrait nommer Christine Lagarde à sa présidence dès novembre, ont déclaré à Reuters quatre sources proches de l'organisation, ce qui impliquerait un départ anticipé de ses fonctions à la tête de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). L’AIE va accélérer la mise sur le marché des stocks de pétrole, dont plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel PARIS, 15 octobre (Reuters) - L’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) est convenue jeudi de mettre sur le marché plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible, ainsi que les volumes restants des réserves d’urgence libérées en mars, afin de contribuer à approvisionner le marché et à freiner la flambée des prix. États-Unis: Les prix à la production enregistrent en septembre leur plus forte hausse en quatre ans et demi 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les prix à la production (PPI) aux États-Unis ont enregistré en septembre leur plus forte hausse en quatre ans et demi, sous l'effet de l'augmentation des coûts des biens et des services, dernier signe en date d'un élargissement des pressions inflationnistes au-delà des produits énergétiques. États-Unis: Les ventes au détail augmentent plus que prévu en septembre avec les prix de l'essence WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les ventes au détail aux Etats-Unis ont augmenté plus que prévu en septembre, portées par la hausse des prix de l'essence, même si les dépenses dans d'autres secteurs sont restées modérées, montrent les données publiées jeudi par le département du Commerce. Alstom prolonge de 15 ans son contrat avec Greater Anglia pour 800 millions de livres sterling 15 octobre (Reuters) - Alstom a annoncé jeudi avoir signé une prolongation de 15 ans de son contrat de maintenance avec l’opérateur ferroviaire britannique Greater Anglia, pour un montant d’environ 800 millions de livres sterling (946,38 millions d'euros). États-Unis: Hausse des inscriptions au chômage à 199.000 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les inscriptions au chômage ont augmenté aux États-Unis, s'établissant à 199.000 lors de la semaine au 10 octobre, a annoncé jeudi le département du Travail. La guerre au Moyen-Orient aura un impact durable sur le commerce - directrice OMC BANGKOK, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les conflits en Ukraine et au Moyen-Orient ainsi que les bouleversements géopolitiques en cours auront un impact durable sur le commerce mondial, a dit jeudi à Reuters Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, directrice générale de l'Organisation mondiale du commerce (OMC). Richemont en discussions pour rejoindre une offre sur le diamantaire De Beers LONDRES/JOHANNESBURG, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Richemont, propriétaire de Cartier, est en discussions pour rejoindre un consortium qui prépare une offre sur le groupe minier diamantaire De Beers mis en vente par Anglo American et dont la valeur est estimée à environ 1 milliard de dollars (892,38 millions d'euros), a déclaré une source proche du dossier. Le fonds souverain norvégien devrait investir dans les géants de la défense - commission OSLO, 15 octobre (Reuters) - La Norvège devrait modifier les règles éthiques de son fonds souverain afin d'investir dans de grands groupes du secteur de la défense, actuellement exclus du portefeuille en raison de leur implication dans la production d'armes nucléaires, a recommandé jeudi une commission désignée par le gouvernement.

item.content:encoded: États-Unis/Midterms: Des enquêtes sur l'empire Trump se profilent au Congrès WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les contributeurs à la construction de la salle de bal du président américain Donald Trump et les partenaires impliqués dans des opérations conclues par des membres de sa famille devraient figurer parmi les premières cibles d'enquêtes si les démocrates reprennent le contrôle de la Chambre des représentants ou du Sénat lors des élections de mi-mandat de novembre, selon plusieurs sources parlementaires et juridiques. Yémen: Explosions près du palais présidentiel à Aden, attaqué par les Houthis 15 octobre (Reuters) - Deux officiers de sécurité ont été tués jeudi au Yémen dans une attaque au missile contre le palais présidentiel à Aden, dans le sud du pays, ont déclaré à Reuters deux représentants du gouvernement, rapportant que les Houthis avaient tiré plusieurs missiles en direction du bâtiment. L'exécution de l'auteur de la fusillade de Ford Hood ne sera pas diffusée en direct, dit Trump WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - - Le président américain Donald Trump a déclaré jeudi que l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, condamné à mort pour le meurtre de 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ne serait finalement pas diffusée en direct. Le sommet UE-Golfe prévu le 24/10 à Ryad est reporté RYAD/BRUXELLES, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le sommet prévu le 24 octobre à Ryad entre l'Union européenne et le Conseil de coopération du Golfe (CCG) a été reporté jeudi pour des raisons de sécurité, en raison notamment des attaques répétées des Houthis contre l'Arabie saoudite qui perturbent le trafic aérien. Moscou construit une base de lancement de drones à réaction en un temps record LONDRES, 15 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a quasiment achevé la construction d'une nouvelle base destinée au lancement de drones à réaction en à peine six semaines, selon des experts de la défense et une analyse de Reuters fondée sur des images satellites, dernier exemple de l'expansion de ses capacités de frappe à proximité de l'Ukraine. Le réseau Starshield rétabli en Ukraine, selon une source KYIV, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le réseau de satellites à usage militaire Starshield, développé par SpaceX, a été pleinement rétabli en Ukraine, a déclaré jeudi une source au sein du ministère ukrainien de la Défense, au lendemain de restrictions imposées à ce service essentiel aux forces de Kyiv. Le toit d'une école s'effondre au Pakistan, 32 enfants tués ISLAMABAD, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Trente-deux enfants ainsi qu'une enseignante ont été tués jeudi au Pakistan par l'effondrement du toit de leur école à Peshawar, rapportent la police et les secours. L'Europe incapable de suppléer aux dysfonctionnements de Starlink en Ukraine 15 octobre (Reuters) - A cours d'une semaine où l'Ukraine a dû faire face à des restrictions du réseau satellitaire Starlink et à l'absence de données américaines la renseignant de l'imminence de frappes de missiles balistiques russes, Kyiv se rend à l'évidence que l'Europe n'est pas en mesure d'offrir la moindre alternative. Roumanie-Deux bateaux en feu en mer Noire, sept marins portés disparus BUCAREST, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Des équipes de secours roumaines sont à la recherche de sept membres d'équipage d'un des deux chimiquiers qui ont pris feu jeudi à la limite des eaux territoriales de la Roumanie en mer Noire, incident qui coïncide avec la détection d'une présence de drones russes dans l'espace aérien roumain, ont dit les autorités du pays. La marine ukrainienne dit avoir endommagé six avions de combat russes 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée ukrainienne a affirmé jeudi avoir endommagé à des degrés divers six chasseurs-bombardiers russes Su-34M lors d'une frappe nocturne sur l'aérodrome de Borissoglebsk, dans la région russe de Voronej.
